cards.action: I architected a framework where AI models are pluggable modules, allowing us to deploy new models like DeepSeek R1 within 24 hours. I also directed the creation of anura, an OpenAI-compatible gateway with automated LiteLLM failover to ensure service stability.
cards.result: This provided drop-in compatibility with LangChain and Autonolas agents. If a decentralized GPU node fails, the failover layer transparently reroutes requests to redundant endpoints without disconnecting the client.
cards.metric: Because models were pluggable Git-versioned modules, our ecosystem could deploy DeepSeek R1 or Wan2.1 Video within 24 hours of release without touching the core Go solver daemon.

cards.project: Nexus: secret scan before upload
cards.her_role: built, led and directed; AI agents wrote the code under my direction
cards.situation: Credentials were present in real repos, so a secret scan before upload was mandatory. On the pilot, the scan of the HTML that would be uploaded found 15 findings, but the same content as raw text found 47.
cards.task: Find why the scanner under-reported, and make sure no secret reached the index.
cards.action: Traced it to HTML entity escaping, which hid the credentials from gitleaks. The scanner was changed to scan the unescaped raw text, and the rule became: scan both copies and require both clean. Every flagged document was dropped and recorded, then re-scanned to zero. An automated PR review then found five fail-open paths, where a failure still reported success: a failed import batch recorded as finished, a pagination error read as end of list, a crashed verification scan read as zero findings, failed clones not failing the harvest, and an existing search app not checked for its stores. All were fixed, and reconcile now checks the manifest. A 403 on the new project looked like a missing role but was IAM propagation; a retry returned 200 and it was recorded as a field finding. I built and led it, directing AI agents that wrote the code; I set the outcome, the gates and the decisions.
cards.result: On the full harvest the scan found 483 findings; 217 documents were dropped, the re-scan came back at 0, and 16,555 clean documents were uploaded.

cards.topic: upfront technical design: identity, data boundary, residency and legal
cards.project: Nexus: upfront design for indexing her GitHub estate into Google Agent Search
cards.her_role: built, led and directed; AI agents wrote the code under my direction
cards.situation: Before building Nexus, I had to decide how the solution would integrate with the customer's sources, identity, data boundary and budget, and record each decision so it could be challenged.
cards.task: Design the integration upfront: which connector, which identity, where the data lives, and what content had the right to be indexed at all.
cards.action: I chose a custom harvester over the native GitHub connector, because the connector needs a Gemini Enterprise setup and licence, and a harvester gives control over eligibility, secret scanning and document shape. For identity, production authenticates through Workload Identity Federation to a dedicated service account holding only roles/discoveryengine.editor, with no keys. I limited the index to customer-owned code: client-owned repositories were excluded even though I had access, because access is not the same as the right to index into a new system. I flagged the data store location, global, as the first thing to change for a customer with an in-region residency requirement, since a data store's location is fixed.
cards.result: The secret scan found 483 findings across the full corpus; all 217 affected documents were quarantined locally and never uploaded. Because the search app mixes public, private and internal content, every document carries visibility in its metadata, and the design requires queries filtered to public before any live demo.
cards.metric: 483 secret findings; 217 documents quarantined and never uploaded.

cards.project: Verifying GPU work on untrusted nodes (Lilypad research, arXiv:2501.05374)
cards.situation: Lilypad ran AI jobs on GPU nodes nobody controlled, so we had to prove the work was really done.
cards.task: Find a verification method that works for non-deterministic GPU workloads.
cards.action: We assessed the options and ruled out three: exact recomputation fails on non-determinism, TEEs are hardware-bound, FHE costs too much. We also analysed zero-knowledge and TEE approaches: a SNARK circuit cannot execute an external binary, so we restructured the problem.
cards.result: We proposed two probabilistic frameworks: a binary reference model with trusted-node checks, and a ternary consensus model with no trust needed. Published on arXiv, January 2025, Boniardi, Bishop, Haire.
cards.metric: 3 approaches assessed and ruled out, 2 frameworks proposed.

cards.project: Livepeer docs: local preview taking 5+ minutes
cards.situation: In the Livepeer docs repo, local dev startup was often 5+ minutes, and route changes were slow or crashed, on a large multilingual docs config.
cards.task: Restore iteration speed for maintainers without changing the production docs config.
cards.action: I directed the agent that diagnosed and fixed it. The diagnosis pinned it to the size of the full multilingual docs config, with stale concurrent Mint processes raising local failure rates. The fix was scoped dev profiles so a maintainer loads only one version, language and tab, plus a unit test, then a performance baseline script.
cards.result: Both PRs merged (livepeer/docs #789, 4 Mar 2026, and #791, 8 Mar 2026); issue #788 closed.
